transcript: You installed an NPM package just last week. Since then, it has been sending your environment variables to a server you've never heard of. Your database credentials, your API keys, your Stripe secret, your Jot signing key. All of it read from process.env and posted to an external endpoint every time your application starts up. The package had 50,000 weekly downloads. The name was one character off from the real one. So you installed it because your AI recommended it and you never checked. So your dependency list is an attack surface. Every package on it is code you did not write running with full access to your environment. So let's get this cleaned up. Step 1, a dependency audit on every package in your lock file. Not just your direct dependencies, your transitive dependencies, the package your package is installed. A single application can pull in 800 packages from a dozen maintainers you have never ever heard of. Direct your AI to run a full dependency tree audit.Flag any package with fewer than 100 weekly downloads, any package where the maintainer changed in the last 90 days, and any package with post-install scripts that execute on install. Injections are not cool. That's the win if you run that program. Step two, environment variable isolation. Your application should not expose every environment variable to every process. Secrets needed by one module should not be readable by every package in the dependency tree. So direct your AI to implement scoped secret access where each module receives only the environment variables that it needs, not the full process dot EMV object that's a win and step 3 lock file integrity verification on CI your lock file pins exact versions if a dependency is modified upstream after you installed it the checksum will not match your CI pipeline should verify lock file integrity on every build and reject any build where the checksums do not match the expected values. So direct your AI to configure lock file integrity up checks in your CI pipeline that block deployment on any checksum mismatch. Your code is only as trustworthy as your least trusted dependency. So audit the list before the list is auditing you.

claims.topic: NPM dependency supply-chain risk, secret exposure, and lockfile integrity controls
claims.problem: The transcript frames an NPM dependency list as an application attack surface: a mistakenly installed, malicious, typo-squatted, or compromised package can run third-party code with access to application environment variables and may exfiltrate credentials unless dependencies, secret exposure, and build integrity are controlled.
technicalClaims: Claim: A malicious NPM package can read sensitive values from Node.js `process.env` and send them to an external endpoint when application code starts, exposing database credentials, API keys, payment secrets, and signing keys if those values are present in the process environment.

Claim: An application's NPM dependency list is an attack surface because direct and transitive packages are third-party code running with application-level access; a single application can pull in hundreds of packages from maintainers the application team may not know.

Claim: Typo-squatted packages with names close to legitimate packages can be installed accidentally, especially if a developer accepts an AI-recommended package name without independently checking it.

Claim: Packages with fewer than 100 weekly downloads, packages whose maintainer changed in the last 90 days, and packages with install-time scripts are presented as dependency-audit risk signals; post-install scripts are specifically risky because they execute code during package installation.

Claim: Lockfile integrity checks in CI can detect dependency content that no longer matches the expected checksum for the pinned dependency version, and builds with checksum mismatches should be rejected to prevent deployment of modified dependency artifacts.
claims.recommendedSolution: Treat the dependency list as an attack surface and test the following controls: run a full dependency tree audit over every package in the lockfile, including direct and transitive dependencies; flag packages with fewer than 100 weekly downloads, recent maintainer changes within 90 days, or post-install scripts; implement scoped secret access so modules receive only the environment variables they need rather than unrestricted access to the full `process.env` object; and configure CI to verify lockfile integrity checksums on every build and block deployment when checksums do not match expected values.
reasoning: If a third-party package is installed into a Node.js application, its code may execute with the same process privileges as application code; if secrets are stored in `process.env`, the package can allegedly read those secrets and send them elsewhere.

A typo-squatted package name that differs by one character can be mistaken for a legitimate package; accepting an AI recommendation without manual verification increases the chance that the wrong package enters the dependency graph.

Auditing only direct dependencies leaves transitive dependencies unchecked, even though transitive packages can also execute code and may be maintained by unknown parties; auditing the full lockfile is intended to reveal risk indicators across the entire installed tree.

The proposed audit heuristics are not presented as proof of compromise; they are warning signals. Low download count may indicate obscure or less-reviewed packages, recent maintainer changes may indicate possible ownership-risk changes, and post-install scripts are notable because they can run code before the application itself starts.

Restricting modules to only the secrets they need is intended to reduce blast radius: a dependency that does not receive a particular secret should not be able to read and exfiltrate that secret through ordinary module inputs.

Lockfiles pin exact dependency versions and include integrity metadata; CI verification compares resolved package artifacts against expected checksums, so a mismatch is treated as evidence that the artifact is not the one the build expected.
assumptions: The application is a Node.js/NPM application that installs dependencies from the NPM ecosystem and uses a lockfile with integrity metadata.
Sensitive credentials such as database credentials, API keys, Stripe secrets, or JWT signing keys are present in environment variables available to the application process.
Installed dependency code, including transitive dependency code or install scripts, can execute in an environment where it has network access or another way to exfiltrate data.

The repository and build system expose enough information to enumerate direct and transitive dependencies from a lockfile and to inspect package metadata such as download counts, maintainer changes, and lifecycle scripts.
The runtime architecture can be changed so modules receive scoped configuration or secret values instead of relying directly on global `process.env` access.
CI has access to the package manager's lockfile integrity data and can be configured to fail builds on checksum or integrity mismatches.
technologiesAndPatterns: NPM lockfile / package lock integrity metadata
Direct and transitive dependency tree auditing
NPM lifecycle scripts, especially post-install scripts
Scoped secret access / least-privilege configuration injection
AI-assisted development/package recommendation as a source of unverified dependency selection

implications.detail: Third-party dependency code may have access to secrets stored in process-level environment variables, so a malicious or compromised package could exfiltrate credentials.
Transitive dependencies expand the attack surface beyond the packages explicitly chosen by developers, because they may run code from many maintainers not directly reviewed by the team.
Typo-squatted packages are a supply-chain risk when package names are accepted without verification, including when suggested by an AI tool.
Install-time lifecycle scripts increase supply-chain exposure because code can execute during dependency installation, not only during application runtime.
Failing CI on lockfile checksum mismatches may prevent builds from deploying when dependency artifacts differ from the expected lockfile integrity values.
Implementing scoped secret access may require refactoring modules that currently read from global `process.env` directly.
Adding dependency-audit and integrity gates may introduce review work and build failures that developers must triage, especially for low-download packages, maintainer changes, and lifecycle scripts.

uncertainties: Repository inspection can determine whether the project uses NPM, which dependencies and transitive dependencies are listed in the lockfile, whether lifecycle scripts are present, and whether CI contains lockfile integrity checks.

Repository inspection can identify direct uses of `process.env` and whether modules receive scoped configuration, but it may not prove which secrets are actually present in production environment variables.
Package download counts and maintainer-change history require external registry or package metadata; they may not be fully inferable from the repository alone.

Whether any installed package is actually malicious, typo-squatted, compromised, or exfiltrating secrets requires package-source review, network/runtime observation, incident evidence, or threat-intelligence data beyond a simple repository audit.

Whether CI checksum verification catches all relevant upstream modification scenarios depends on the package manager behavior, lockfile contents, registry behavior, cache configuration, and how dependencies are installed in CI.
The transcript presents thresholds such as fewer than 100 weekly downloads and maintainer changes within 90 days as flags, not as validated indicators that a package is unsafe.

onboardingPrompt:
You are a capable coding agent with repository access. Your task is read-only onboarding for a later audit about NPM dependency supply-chain exposure, environment-based secret handling, and package-lock/build integrity. Do not test or advocate any proposed fix yet, do not assert that a vulnerability exists, and do not edit, install, update, refactor, or commit anything.

Operational constraints:
- Use static repository inspection first. If you run commands, they must be read-only and must not install packages or execute package lifecycle scripts. Avoid `npm install`, `npm ci`, or package-manager commands that may run scripts. Prefer file inspection and safe parsing of manifests/lockfiles.
- Record exact evidence: file paths plus precise symbols, scripts, workflow names, routes, schemas, settings, lockfile fields, or traced flows.
- Separate Confirmed facts from Inference and Unknowns. If something depends on production runtime, external registry metadata, traffic, CI execution, or secrets that are not in the repo, say so.

Discover the current system before any later recommendation is evaluated.

1. Repository and runtime boundaries
Map the repository layout and identify which parts are Node.js/NPM applications, packages, functions, workers, CLIs, frontend bundles, backend services, or build-only tooling. Note monorepos/workspaces and package boundaries. Identify likely runtime entrypoints such as server startup files, serverless handlers, job runners, Docker/Procfile commands, package scripts, framework conventions, or deployment descriptors. Include ownership boundaries if CODEOWNERS, service catalogs, docs, or team labels exist.

2. Package-management architecture
Identify the package manager and lockfile model actually used: `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, `npm-shrinkwrap.json`, `yarn.lock`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, workspace manifests, `.npmrc`, registry settings, overrides/resolutions, package-manager pins, and Node/NPM version constraints. List root and workspace package manifests and the important install/build/test scripts. Note whether dependencies are separated into production, development, peer, optional, and bundled categories. Do not perform a full risk audit yet; just map where the dependency graph and install behavior are defined.

3. Configuration and secret-flow architecture
Map how configuration enters the application: direct `process.env` reads, config modules, schema validators, dotenv usage, secret-manager clients, framework config, container/Kubernetes/serverless env declarations, CI secrets references, and test fixtures. Identify exact files/symbols where environment variables are read and whether values are centralized, validated, passed as explicit configuration objects, or accessed ad hoc across modules. Do not infer that any named variable is a real production secret unless repository evidence or deployment config supports that.

4. Request, data, and control flows relevant to third-party code
Trace the high-level control flow from process startup through dependency imports, framework initialization, route/handler registration, background jobs, build steps, and test harnesses. Identify where third-party packages are imported by runtime code versus only build/test tooling where this is statically visible. Map outbound network capabilities and infrastructure controls only if repository evidence exists, such as HTTP clients, SDKs, proxy settings, egress/network policies, VPC/serverless config, or container definitions.

5. CI/CD and build integrity architecture
Map CI workflows and deployment pipelines that install dependencies, restore caches, build artifacts, run tests, publish images/packages, or deploy. Identify exact workflow files and install commands, whether lockfiles are required, whether caches include `node_modules` or package-manager caches, and whether any existing jobs appear to check dependency integrity, audit dependencies, scan secrets, or enforce package policies. Record where build failures would block deployment, if inferable.

6. Tests and observability
Identify tests, linters, scanners, policy checks, and observability signals materially relevant to dependency installation, dependency review, env/config handling, secret scanning, network egress, and CI reliability. Include test file paths and job names. Note runtime evidence that is unavailable from the repository, such as production env contents, CI logs, registry responses, dependency download counts, maintainer history, network traces, or checksum-failure behavior.

Deliverable: Produce a concise architecture briefing with these sections:
- System map: services/packages, entrypoints, runtime/build boundaries.
- Dependency/package-management map: manifests, lockfiles, workspaces, scripts, registry/config settings.
- Config and secret-flow map: env variable access points, config modules, deployment/CI secret references.
- CI/build map: install commands, lockfile use, caches, deployment gates, existing checks.
- Tests/observability map: relevant checks and missing runtime signals.
- Confirmed facts vs inferences vs unknowns.
- Handoff map for the follow-up audit: exact files/symbols/workflows to inspect next, safe read-only commands that could be run without installing/executing dependencies, and external/runtime evidence that would be needed.

Stop after the briefing and wait for the next prompt. Do not recommend changes or evaluate the video claims yet.
investigationPrompt:
You are a capable coding agent with repository access. Continue from the onboarding briefing if available. Your task is a read-only, evidence-backed investigation of a dependency supply-chain and secret-exposure hypothesis for a Node.js/NPM-style project. Do not edit files, install packages, execute dependency lifecycle scripts, create commits, or implement fixes.

Hypothesis to evaluate, with qualifications preserved:
- The dependency list should be treated as application attack surface because direct and transitive NPM packages are third-party code that may run with application-level privileges.
- If sensitive values are present in the Node.js process environment, malicious or compromised package code may be able to read `process.env` and exfiltrate those values through network or other output paths.
- Accidental installation of typo-squatted packages is possible, including when a developer accepts an AI-suggested package name without independent verification.
- A full dependency-tree audit over the lockfile may reveal risk signals across both direct and transitive dependencies. The proposed signals are fewer than 100 weekly downloads, maintainer change within the last 90 days, and lifecycle/install scripts, especially post-install scripts. These are warning signals, not proof of compromise.
- Scoped configuration or secret access is proposed to reduce blast radius by passing modules only the values they need instead of relying on unrestricted application use of global `process.env`. Evaluate whether that is technically meaningful in this repository; do not assume it sandboxes arbitrary third-party code running in the same process.
- CI should verify lockfile integrity checksums on every build and reject builds when resolved package artifacts do not match expected lockfile integrity metadata. Evaluate whether current package-manager behavior and CI commands already provide this, whether it is bypassed, and what cannot be proven statically.

Evidence and status rules:
For every material claim, provide an applicability status: Confirmed, Partially Applicable, Refuted, Not Applicable, or Needs Runtime Verification. Include exact static repository evidence, missing evidence, assumptions, realistic impact, confidence, and severity where meaningful. Severity must be Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Informational based on actual exposure, package reachability, secret sensitivity, frequency, scale, exploitability, reliability impact, and operational cost. Do not inflate a theoretical supply-chain concern into a production incident without evidence.

Explicitly separate:
- Static evidence: repository files, lockfile metadata, manifests, imports, scripts, CI YAML, deployment descriptors, config code, tests, scanners.
- External metadata: NPM registry download counts, maintainer-change history, package provenance/advisories, threat intelligence.
- Runtime evidence: production env contents, CI execution logs, install traces, cache behavior, checksum-failure tests, network egress logs, package runtime behavior, telemetry, profiling, or traffic characteristics.
Never fabricate external or runtime results. If they are unavailable, mark the claim Needs Runtime Verification or Needs External Metadata and state exactly what evidence would settle it.

Investigation methodology

1. Applicability and package-manager baseline
Determine whether the repository actually contains a Node.js/NPM application or package. If it uses Yarn, pnpm, vendored dependencies, no lockfile, or only frontend/build tooling, adapt the analysis and mark NPM-specific claims accordingly. Inspect `package.json`, workspace manifests, lockfiles, `.npmrc`, `engines`, `packageManager`, Dockerfiles, CI workflows, and deployment configs. Confirm:
- package manager and version expectations;
- lockfile type/version and whether integrity metadata is present;
- root/workspace structure and production versus dev dependency boundaries;
- install/build/test commands used locally and in CI;
- registries, scopes, overrides/resolutions, dependency pinning, and cache behavior.

2. Direct and transitive dependency attack-surface inventory
From lockfile/manifests, inventory the dependency graph as far as static evidence permits. Include counts for direct production, direct development, transitive, optional, peer, and workspace/internal packages if feasible. Identify dependencies that are likely runtime-reachable by tracing imports from server/client/job entrypoints and distinguishing them from build/test-only tooling. If full static reachability is not feasible, sample critical paths and state limits.

For the claim that a single app may pull hundreds of third-party packages, report the actual lockfile/package counts and whether that exposure applies to runtime, build time, test time, or all install contexts. Counterevidence may include tiny dependency graphs, vendoring, internal-only packages, no Node runtime, or strict isolated build stages.

3. Lifecycle script and install-time execution review
Inspect lockfile indicators such as `hasInstallScript`, package manifests available in the repo, `scripts` in root/workspaces, `.npmrc` settings, CI install flags, and package-manager config. Identify packages or workspace scripts that can run during install, prepare, preinstall, install, postinstall, prepack, or build phases. Do not execute them. Determine whether CI uses controls such as `--ignore-scripts`, trusted builders, isolated containers, no secrets during install, restricted networking, or policy tooling. If lockfile does not expose lifecycle script details and `node_modules` is absent, note the missing package metadata rather than guessing.

4. Risk-signal audit for low downloads, maintainer changes, and typo-squatting
Treat these as heuristic signals only. Static repository inspection can identify package names, versions, scopes, and whether package choices are documented or reviewed. It generally cannot establish weekly download counts or maintainer changes. If network/external lookups are allowed by your environment, use read-only registry queries and record source, time, package, version, and result; otherwise produce a package list requiring external metadata.

Checks to perform:
- Low downloads: flag packages with fewer than 100 weekly downloads only when reliable registry data is available. Distinguish internal/private packages, scoped packages, deprecated packages, and packages used only in dev/build.
- Maintainer change within 90 days: require registry/npm profile/package metadata or other trusted external evidence. Mark as Needs External Metadata if unavailable.
- Typo-squatting: compare dependency names against known intended packages where repository evidence exists, such as docs, imports, comments, migration notes, lockfile history, or adjacent popular package names. Similarity alone is not proof. Look for suspicious near-matches, unexpected scopes, unused dependencies, abandoned replacements, or package names inconsistent with imports. AI-assisted selection is only assessable if repository history, PR text, comments, or docs mention it; otherwise mark Unknown/Not evidenced.

5. Secret and `process.env` exposure analysis
Inventory all application `process.env` access points and config abstractions with file paths and symbols. Classify variables by apparent sensitivity using names and context, but avoid asserting production secret presence without deployment/secret-manager evidence. Trace how config values are passed into modules, clients, SDKs, database adapters, auth/payment integrations, and route/job handlers.

Evaluate these questions:
- Are secrets likely present in the Node process environment at runtime, based on deployment descriptors, CI secret injection, Docker/Kubernetes/serverless config, secret-manager clients, or docs?
- Is config centralized and validated, or do arbitrary modules read `process.env` directly?
- Do third-party dependencies run in the same Node process as code that has these env vars?
- Are secrets available during dependency installation in CI/build containers, or only at runtime/deploy time?
- Are there egress controls, proxies, network policies, serverless VPC settings, container restrictions, or audit logs that would limit or detect exfiltration?

Important causal-fit check: Passing explicit config objects to first-party modules can improve maintainability and reduce accidental first-party secret spread, but it does not by itself prevent a malicious package loaded in the same Node process from reading global `process.env` unless the runtime environment is actually changed, secrets are not present, the dependency is isolated/sandboxed, or other controls apply. Preserve this nuance in the recommendation assessment.

6. Lockfile integrity and CI enforcement
Inspect lockfile integrity fields and CI/package-manager behavior. Confirm whether builds use committed lockfiles and deterministic install commands such as `npm ci` rather than lockfile-mutating commands. Check whether CI fails on install errors before deployment, whether deployment depends on those jobs, and whether caches could bypass integrity verification by reusing `node_modules` without reinstalling. Inspect `.npmrc` for settings that affect lockfiles, scripts, registry, strict SSL, audit, package-lock use, or offline/cache behavior.

Assess what can be established statically: presence of integrity metadata, install command selection, pipeline gating, and cache strategy. Assess what requires runtime proof: actual checksum mismatch behavior, registry/cache artifact resolution, CI logs, package-manager version behavior, and whether every deployment path runs the check. Do not alter the lockfile to simulate a mismatch unless explicitly authorized; instead state the safe test that would be needed.

7. Current mitigations, counterevidence, and constraints
Identify existing controls and their scope: Dependabot/Renovate, npm audit, Snyk/Socket/OSV, lockfile-lint, package provenance/signature checks, secret scanning, CODEOWNERS/review rules, dependency allowlists, private registries, `--ignore-scripts`, build isolation, no secrets in CI install steps, network egress restrictions, container hardening, SBOM generation, and monitoring. Also identify constraints and likely side effects: false positives from low-download thresholds, native packages requiring install scripts, private/internal packages without public download data, monorepo workspace quirks, developer triage burden, CI duration, and refactoring cost for config injection.

8. Recommendation fit and alternatives
For each proposed control, determine whether to Proceed, Modify, Reject, or Gather More Evidence:
- Full lockfile audit: fit to graph size, runtime/build distinction, existing tooling, and review capacity.
- Low-download/recent-maintainer/install-script flags: usefulness as triage signals, false-positive risk, and data availability.
- Scoped secret access: fit to current config architecture and whether it materially reduces exposure in same-process Node execution; consider stronger or smaller alternatives such as reducing env secrets present in the process, late secret retrieval, process isolation, sandboxing, egress controls, secret redaction/logging controls, or central config validation.
- CI checksum enforcement: whether existing deterministic install and integrity verification are sufficient, need hardening, or need runtime validation.

Report format
Produce a concise evidence-backed report with:
1. Executive summary: overall disposition: Proceed, Modify Recommendation, Reject, or Gather More Evidence, with 3-6 bullets of rationale.
2. Evidence matrix for material claims with columns: Claim/control, Status, Severity, Static evidence, Missing external/runtime evidence, Assumptions, Impact, Confidence.
3. Dependency findings: package-manager baseline, direct/transitive counts, runtime versus build/test distinction, lifecycle script indicators, typo-squat observations, and external metadata gaps.
4. Secret exposure findings: `process.env` inventory, config flow, apparent secret categories, same-process dependency exposure, install-time secret exposure, egress/observability controls, and limits of static proof.
5. Lockfile/CI integrity findings: lockfile metadata, CI install commands, gates, caches, existing checks, and runtime verification needed.
6. Current mitigations and counterevidence.
7. Recommendation assessment: proceed/modify/reject/gather-evidence for each proposed control, side effects, operational cost, and smaller/safer alternatives.
8. Areas that should remain untouched in any future work, open questions, and exact runtime/external evidence needed next.

End with STOP. Do not provide implementation code, patches, commits, or refactors.
